findings.claim: Anchoring (over-weighting the first information encountered)
findings.failure_mode: definition swapped for the canonical Tversky-Kahneman gloss; the source defines anchoring as focus on one particular piece of information, with no 'first'
findings.evidence: Deep 144 [V]: 'tendency to focus on one particular piece of information when making decisions or problem-solving'. Source 12926-12927: 'An anchoring bias occurs when you focus on one piece of information when making a decision or solving a problem'.
findings.fix: correct: Anchoring (fixing on one particular piece of information)

findings.claim: availability (judging frequency or probability by how readily examples come to mind)
findings.failure_mode: definition swapped for the canonical Tversky-Kahneman gloss; the source says nothing about judging frequency or probability
findings.evidence: Deep 148 [V]: 'decision is based upon either an available precedent or an example that may be faulty'. Source 12953-12955: 'a decision based on an example, information, or recent experience that is ... readily available to you, even though it may not be the best example'.
findings.fix: correct: availability (deciding from a readily available precedent or example that may be faulty)

findings.section: Key Concepts 3 (Mental set and functional fixedness)
findings.claim: Functional fixedness is the inability to perceive an object or strategy as usable for something other than its designed purpose.
findings.failure_mode: concept widened: the source's functional fixedness concerns objects only; 'or strategy' is the distillation's extension presented as definition
findings.evidence: Deep 150: 'inability to perceive an object being used for something other than its designed purpose'. Source (Ch 7.3 'Pitfalls to Problem Solving'): 'you cannot perceive an object being used for something other than what it was designed for'.
findings.fix: correct: Functional fixedness is the inability to perceive an object as usable for something other than its designed purpose; the decision-making analogue is treating a strategy the same way.

findings.claim: Counters: external opinions, private voting, leaders withholding initial positions, devil's advocate roles. (Source: Ch 12.4)
findings.failure_mode: list item imported and attributed to the source: 'devil's advocate' does not occur in the source; the source's contingency planning is dropped
findings.evidence: Deep 295: 'external opinions, private voting, leaders withholding initial positions, and contingency planning'. Source 23790-23794 lists outside opinions, private voting, leader withholding position, research on all viewpoints, weighing costs and benefits, contingency plan. grep 'devil' finds no such use.
findings.fix: correct: Counters: external opinions, private voting, leaders withholding initial positions until all members have spoken, and contingency planning.

findings.claim: The bystander effect (diffusion of responsibility) is the same mechanism applied to helping decisions.
findings.failure_mode: equivalence the source does not draw: social loafing is explained by non-evaluation of individual effort; diffusion of responsibility is the bystander-effect mechanism
findings.evidence: Source 23839-23840 (Ch 12.4): 'Because each individual's efforts are not evaluated, individuals can become less motivated to perform well'. Deep 295 (loafing) and 303 (bystander, diffusion of responsibility, Ch 12.6) are separate.
findings.fix: correct: The bystander effect (diffusion of responsibility, Ch 12.6) is a related group-size effect on helping decisions.

findings.claim: Strong emotion narrows attention and pushes processing toward heuristic, type-1 modes.
findings.failure_mode: claim smuggled from dual-process literature: neither the deep ref nor the source links arousal or emotion to attention-narrowing or heuristic use, and 'type-1' is not source vocabulary
findings.evidence: Deep 228: Yerkes-Dodson (performance vs arousal by task complexity) only. Deep 138: the five conditions that invoke heuristics (information overload, time pressure, low stakes, limited information, a heuristic comes to mind) do not include arousal. No 'type 1'/'System 1'/'dual process' in source.
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: (Source: Ch 10.1, "Arousal Theory")
findings.failure_mode: mis-cited section: Ch 10.1 has no 'Arousal Theory' heading; Yerkes-Dodson sits under 'Theories About Motivation', and 'arousal theory' as a bolded term belongs to Ch 8 (emotion and memory strength)
findings.evidence: Source 18751-18772 (Yerkes-Dodson) under heading 'Theories About Motivation'; 'arousal theory' bolded at 14794 (Ch 8).
findings.fix: correct: (Source: Ch 10.1, "Theories About Motivation")

findings.claim: Self-efficacy is shaped by past performance, vicarious experience, social persuasion, and physiological state.
findings.failure_mode: Bandura's four-sources model imported from outside the source; the source says only that self-efficacy may include previous successful completion and is 'developed through our social experiences'
findings.evidence: Deep 19, 228, 257: definition and effects only. Source 18778-18779 (Ch 10.1) and 21292-21293 (Ch 11.4). No 'vicarious experience', 'social persuasion', 'verbal persuasion' or 'physiological state' in the self-efficacy passages.
findings.fix: correct: Self-efficacy can rest on previous success at the same or a similar task and is developed through social experience (Ch 10.1; Ch 11.4) | cycle-to-deep: source 18778-18779 and 21292-21303 (developed through social experiences; high vs low self-efficacy and challenging tasks)

findings.section: What to Look For (Group consensus emerges too smoothly)
findings.claim: Diagnosis: groupthink or pluralistic ignorance.
findings.failure_mode: concept not in the deep ref or the source ('pluralistic' does not occur in the source)
findings.evidence: grep -i 'pluralistic' in sources/converted/openstax-psychology-2e.md: 0 hits; absent from deep ref.
findings.fix: correct: Diagnosis: groupthink (illusion of unanimity, self-censorship).

findings.section: What to Look For (Hiring or evaluation patterns with group membership)
findings.claim: Follow-up: structured interviews; standardised criteria; blind evaluation where possible; counter-stereotypic exemplar exposure.
findings.failure_mode: applied guidance partly resting on a premise the source does not carry: counter-stereotypic exemplar exposure as an implicit-bias remedy is not in the source text (the phrase appears only in a reference-list title)
findings.evidence: Deep 325 and source 25962-25970 support structured interviews. Deep 299, 351 give superordinate goals and intergroup contact under equal status, common goals, cooperation and institutional support (Pettigrew and Tropp) as prejudice reducers.
findings.fix: correct: Follow-up: structured interviews (Ch 13.2); standardised criteria; blind evaluation where possible; intergroup contact under equal status and common goals (Ch 13.3).

findings.claim: The chair notes that her arousal is pushing toward a heuristic ("the numbers say no")
findings.failure_mode: turns on the unsupported arousal-to-heuristic premise (D006); the source's heuristic triggers are overload, time pressure, low stakes, limited information
findings.evidence: Deep 138 (five conditions); deep 228 (Yerkes-Dodson concerns performance, not heuristic use).
findings.fix: correct: The chair notes that her arousal is higher than suits a complex decision (Yerkes-Dodson) and that time pressure is pushing her toward a heuristic ("the numbers say no")

findings.claim: a precommitment against escalation of commitment and confirmation bias
findings.failure_mode: concept imported from another corpus source without citation: escalation of commitment is not in the Psychology 2e deep ref or source; it is barrier 2 in OpenStax Organizational Behavior Ch 6.4
findings.evidence: Psych source: 'escalation' occurs only in the workplace-violence passage. OB deep 186: 'Escalation of commitment: decision-makers stay committed to poor decisions even as costs mount'.
findings.fix: correct: a precommitment against confirmation bias (and against escalation of commitment, per OpenStax Organizational Behavior Ch 6.4)

findings.claim: This worked example illustrates ... heuristic-versus-systematic processing ... fundamental attribution error and actor-observer asymmetry applied to performance evaluation
findings.failure_mode: concepts mislabelled: the example's pattern (board members read the CEO's failure dispositionally and the CEO's success situationally) is not actor-observer bias, which contrasts one's own behaviour with others'; and 'systematic processing' is Organizational Behavior's vocabulary, the source's contrast is heuristics vs algorithms
findings.evidence: Deep 277: actor-observer bias = others dispositional, own behaviour situational; FAE = overweighting dispositional explanations of others. Deep 138: trial and error, algorithms, heuristics. OB deep 179: 'systematic processing through the reflective system'.
findings.fix: correct: heuristics versus deliberate problem-solving, availability and anchoring biases, the fundamental attribution error applied selectively to performance evaluation, group structuring against premature consensus, and hindsight management in retrospective review

findings.claim: Implicit bias plus the team halo effect plus actor-observer asymmetry produce decisions that pattern with demographics rather than merit.
findings.failure_mode: only implicit bias links to demographic patterning in the source; the team halo effect is about team credit versus individual blame, and actor-observer bias is self versus others
findings.evidence: Source 26765-26767: team halo effect = 'Teams are given credit for their successes, but individuals within a team are blamed for team failures'. Deep 277, 299.
findings.fix: correct: Implicit bias produces decisions that pattern with demographics rather than merit; the team halo effect and actor-observer asymmetry further skew individual evaluation.

findings.claim: OpenStax Psychology 2e describes the cognitive limits Simon's framework names; the heuristics inventory is a list of ways bounded-rational agents cope.
findings.failure_mode: integration row names a framework that neither this source nor its deep ref mentions, without pointing to where the corpus holds it (Simon is borrowed-through OpenStax Organizational Behavior Ch 6.4)
findings.evidence: No 'Simon' (the economist) or 'bounded' in the Psych source. OB deep 185, 688: bounded rationality (Simon) [BT], Ch 6.4.
findings.fix: correct: Bounded rationality (Simon, via OpenStax Organizational Behavior Ch 6.4) | Psychology 2e's heuristics inventory (Ch 7.3) details the shortcuts that OB's bounded-rationality barrier names in outline.

findings.claim: The overjustification effect (Ch 10.1) suggests that adding extrinsic incentives to decisions about intrinsically motivating work erodes engagement.
findings.failure_mode: qualified finding stated without its qualifiers ('can'; tangible more than praise; expected more than surprise; cultural context)
findings.evidence: Deep 226: 'extrinsic rewards can erode intrinsic motivation ... tangible rewards (money) tend to undermine intrinsic motivation more than verbal praise; expected rewards undermine more than surprise rewards; cultural context matters'.
findings.fix: correct: The overjustification effect (Ch 10.1) suggests that adding extrinsic incentives to intrinsically motivating work can erode engagement, more so for tangible and expected rewards than for praise or surprise rewards.

findings.claim: Self-efficacy (Ch 10.1) is a precondition for difficult-goal acceptance
findings.failure_mode: overstated: the source says self-efficacy shapes goal-setting and willingness to take on challenging tasks, not that it is a precondition; Locke and Latham appear in neither Psych 2e deep ref nor source (Locke's goal theory is held via OB Ch 7.3)
findings.evidence: Deep 228 (drives goal-setting and persistence). Source 21298-21302: high self-efficacy people see challenges as tasks to master; low self-efficacy people 'avoid challenging tasks'. OB deep 232: Goal theory (Locke) [BT] (Ch 7.3).
findings.fix: correct: Goal theory (Locke, via OpenStax Organizational Behavior Ch 7.3) | Self-efficacy (Ch 10.1; Ch 11.4) shapes whether people take on challenging goals; decisions to set ambitious goals must account for it.

findings.claim: fair process sustains commitment even when distributive outcomes disappoint
findings.failure_mode: outcome misdescribed: the source's Greenberg study measured theft after full versus curt explanations of a pay rate; it reports nothing about commitment or disappointing outcomes
findings.evidence: Deep 357: 'adequate explanations of pay decisions reduced theft compared to curt explanations' [BT]. Source 26932-26939.
findings.fix: correct: fair, explained process reduces retaliation such as theft (Greenberg's pay-explanation study, Ch 13.3)

findings.claim: The deep reference contains the following [BT] citations
findings.failure_mode: marker provenance misstated for four of fifteen items: the deep ref carries Rotter as [AP], Schacter as [AR]/unmarked, Yerkes-Dodson as [AP], Schachter-Singer unmarked (lines 193-196)
findings.evidence: Deep 257 (Rotter, [AP]); deep 15 and 180-184 (Schacter, [AR] / unmarked); deep 228 (Yerkes-Dodson, [AP]); deep 244 (Schachter-Singer, unmarked).
findings.fix: correct: The following authors are cited by the source but not held as primary references in this corpus (the deep reference marks most [BT]; Rotter and Yerkes-Dodson sit in [AP] passages, Schacter and Schachter-Singer in [AR] or unmarked passages)

findings.claim: Jerrold Greenberg, procedural justice in the workplace
findings.failure_mode: first name supplied from outside the source; the source gives only 'Greenberg (1993)' / 'Greenberg, J. (1993)'
findings.evidence: Source 26932 and reference list 42055. Deep 357: 'Greenberg's experiments'.
findings.fix: correct: Greenberg (1993), procedural justice in the workplace

findings.claim: Key Concepts are drawn from [AP] (the source's stated cognitive framework positions) or [AE] (worked examples and study summaries).
findings.failure_mode: marker account does not match the deep ref: the deep ref uses no [AE] markers, and Key Concepts draw on [V], [BT], [AR] and unmarked passages as well as [AP]
findings.evidence: grep -c '[AE]' in openstax-psychology-2e-deep.md = 0. Key Concepts 2 and 13 rest on [V] (deep 144-148, 19); 7 on [BT] (deep 291).
findings.fix: correct: Key Concepts draw on the deep reference's [V] definitions (Ch 7.3, Table 7.3; Ch 10.1), [AP] framework paraphrases, and [BT] study summaries.

notes: Quotations: all six [V] quotes (four Table 7.3 definitions, 'not always the best method for making a rational decision', the self-efficacy definition) match the converted source; 'confirms' reads 'confrms' in the source (ligature loss). Section cites checked: 'Problem-Solving Strategies' and 'Self-efficacy and Social Motives' exist; 'Arousal Theory' does not (D007). The file adds a '## Verbatim anchors from the source' section that the projection template does not include, and carries no blockquotes; structure only, not graded. Integration checks: OB row matches OB deep 179-186 (six-step process, six barriers); Festinger row matches Ch 12.3. Applied guidance using vocabulary absent from the source ('systematic processing' in the Phase 1 question, 'psychological safety' at line 106, devil's advocate as a follow-up at lines 95/125/151, process-vs-outcome at line 113) was graded FAITHFUL as guidance that is not attributed to the author. Most serious: D006 (arousal-narrows-attention/type-1 claim), D008 (Bandura's four sources imported), D009 (pluralistic ignorance).
